summary: Deep Orbit is a game in which you take a space mission from the drawing board to splashdown. First you design it: with a fixed budget you choose a launch vehicle, fuel tank, power system, antenna and science instruments, while live gauges show money, mass, delta-v, power and data. Every choice costs something: instruments add science but also mass, power draw and data to send home, and sunlight and radio signals fade with the square of distance, so a design that works at the Moon fails at Jupiter. Then you manage and fly the mission yourself with real orbital mechanics: launch windows, limited fuel, landing, drilling samples before your oxygen runs out, and bringing the crew home before their food runs out. At the end a mission report scores the flight and explains what each design choice did, so you can redesign and try again. The solar system uses the real distances and gravity from NASA's Planetary Fact Sheet. It matters because students rarely get to feel these trade-offs: Deep Orbit turns them from abstract ideas into decisions with consequences.
details: What it does and how it works Deep Orbit lets you run a whole space mission. On the Mission Design screen you get the mission's requirements (delta-v needed, sunlight and radio distance at the destination, science goals, budget) and choose a launch vehicle, fuel tank, power system, antenna and science instruments. Gauges show budget, mass, delta-v, power and data, and a design that is over budget or too heavy cannot launch. Then you fly it yourself: gravity from the Sun, eight planets, the Moon and Ceres acts on the spacecraft all the time, fuel follows the rocket equation, and you must use real launch windows. Crew missions continue with a landing, a walk on the surface to drill samples before the oxygen runs out, and the flight home through Earth's re-entry corridor before the food runs out. A mission report then gives a score and explains what each design choice did. The solar system uses the real distances and orbital periods from NASA's Planetary Fact Sheet (1 AU = 800 pixels, 1 year = 300 seconds), and landings use NASA's surface gravity values. Solar power and radio data rate fall with the square of distance, so solar panels work at Mars but not at Jupiter. Benefits and intended impact Students learn mission design by doing it and seeing the result, not by reading about it. There is no single right answer: a cheap, light probe and a heavy, well-equipped one can both score well, and the report shows how to improve. We want players to understand why real missions look the way they do: why outer-planet probes carry nuclear batteries and big dishes, why you cannot launch to Mars any day you like, and why every kilogram matters. Tools Godot Engine 4.7 with GDScript; pixel art drawn by our team; a Python script that generates the sound effects; Git and GitHub; automatic tests in which a test pilot flies every mission. AI tools (Claude and ChatGPT) were used for much of the code, as described in the AI section. How it is creative You do not only pick parts from a menu: you then have to fly the mission your own design made possible, land it, walk on another world and get home. The same choices come back as consequences hours of mission time later. Factors we considered Realism against playability: planets are drawn far too big and heavy so they can be seen and reached, and the part numbers are simplified, but the physical laws are real, and the game says so. Difficulty: a tutorial, missions that unlock one by one, launch advice and an auto-orbit computer. Fairness: the standard design always works, and a late crew can still get home on emergency rations.
